title: Reusable button component with variants and loading state
requirements:
Build a single <Button> component used across a SaaS admin panel (dashboard actions, forms, modals, danger confirmations).
- Support variant prop: primary, secondary, danger, ghost
- Support size prop: sm, md, lg
- Support isLoading prop that shows a spinner and disables interaction while keeping button width stable (no layout jump)
- Support disabled state distinct from loading (disabled = not loading, just inert)
- Support leftIcon / rightIcon slots
- Must render as either a <button> or, via an "as" / asChild pattern, a styled <a> or Next.js <Link> without duplicating styles
- Fully typed props extending native button attributes so onClick, type, form, etc. all just work
acceptanceCriteria: Clicking a loading or disabled button never fires onClick
Variant + size combinations render correct Tailwind classes with no visual regression between states
Button width does not shift when toggling isLoading (spinner replaces label or sits alongside without reflow)
Component forwards ref to the underlying DOM node
Works as a submit button inside a <form> (type="submit" respected)
Passing an invalid variant is caught at compile time by TypeScript, not just at runtime
Icon-only usage (no text children) still exposes an accessible name via aria-label
componentBreakdown:
Button/
  Button.tsx           -- main component, forwardRef, variant/size class maps
  Spinner.tsx           -- small inline SVG spinner, size synced to button size
  buttonVariants.ts      -- cva() or plain lookup object mapping variant/size -> class strings
  Button.types.ts        -- ButtonProps interface
Usage sites: forms (submit), table row actions, modal footers, confirm-danger flows.
stateModel:
Mostly stateless / controlled by parent via props (isLoading, disabled come from outside -- e.g. a mutation's isPending flag).
No internal state needed for the base component. If building a demo harness, keep a local isLoading boolean in the parent story/page to toggle the prop.
Style resolution state: a derived (not stored) class string computed from variant + size + state on every render via a pure function (cva or clsx), never stored in useState.
edgeCases: Rapid double-click while the async action is in-flight (isLoading must guard against re-entrancy)
Long label text wrapping or overflowing a fixed-width button
Icon-only button with no visible text -- must still be accessible
Button used inside a <form> where clicking should NOT submit when isLoading
Dark mode contrast for each variant, especially ghost on light backgrounds
Disabled + loading both true at once -- decide which one wins visually and behaviorally
Button rendered as a Link (as="a") that needs disabled-like behavior even though anchors have no disabled attribute
a11yChecklist: Use native <button> semantics whenever possible instead of a styled <div> with onClick
When rendered as an anchor acting like a disabled button, add aria-disabled="true" and remove href or intercept click, since anchors ignore the disabled attribute
Spinner has aria-hidden="true"; loading state is announced via aria-busy="true" on the button
Maintain visible focus ring (focus-visible) with sufficient contrast for keyboard users
Icon-only buttons require aria-label describing the action
Minimum 44x44px hit target on touch devices for sm size buttons
Color is never the only signal for the danger variant -- rely on icon/label wording too
rubric:
Weak: hardcodes variant classes with if/else chains scattered inline, no ref forwarding, loading state just changes text to "Loading...".
Solid: extracts a variant map (or cva), forwardRef, isLoading disables + shows spinner without layout shift, basic TS typing.
Strong: composes native button attributes generically via ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>, handles the anchor/disabled edge case, adds aria-busy and aria-disabled correctly, prevents double submit.
Excellent: also discusses design-system scalability (how this pattern extends to Input, IconButton, Badge using the same variant engine), covers RTL, and writes a couple of unit tests (renders correct classes, blocks onClick while loading).
interviewerQuestions: How would you extend this to support an "asChild" pattern so it can render as a Next.js Link without duplicating styles?
How do you prevent a double network call if the user clicks twice before isLoading flips to true (race between click and state update)?
How would you unit test that the danger variant applies the right classes without snapshotting the entire DOM?
If this button needs to support a confirmation step (click once to arm, click again to confirm) for destructive actions, how would you model that state?
How would this scale into a full design system with Input, IconButton, and Badge sharing the same variant tokens?

title: Accessible modal/dialog component (focus trap, escape to close, overlay click, ARIA)
requirements:
Build a <Modal> used for things like "confirm delete listing" and "edit payment method" flows in a marketplace admin app.
- Props: isOpen, onClose, title, children, optional footer/actions
- Pressing Escape closes it (unless a "preventClose while submitting" flag is set)
- Clicking the overlay (outside the dialog panel) closes it; clicking inside does not
- Focus moves into the modal on open and is trapped inside it while open (Tab/Shift+Tab cycle within)
- Focus returns to the element that opened the modal when it closes
- Background content is inert to screen readers while modal is open (aria-hidden on siblings or inert attribute)
- Body scroll is locked while modal is open
- Support rendering via a portal so it is not clipped by parent overflow:hidden containers
acceptanceCriteria: Tabbing from the last focusable element inside the modal wraps to the first, and Shift+Tab from the first wraps to the last
Escape key closes the modal unless explicitly disabled during a pending async action
The triggering button regains focus after the modal closes
Screen reader announces the dialog role, an accessible name (title), and treats background content as hidden
Multiple modals can theoretically stack without breaking focus trap logic (or the design explicitly documents single-modal-at-a-time constraint)
Body does not scroll behind the modal, and scrollbar-width compensation avoids layout shift when the scrollbar disappears
Clicking the overlay backdrop closes it, but clicking and dragging a text selection that ends outside does not falsely trigger close
componentBreakdown:
Modal/
  Modal.tsx           -- portal + overlay + panel composition
  useFocusTrap.ts       -- hook that queries focusable elements and wires keydown handler
  useLockBodyScroll.ts   -- hook to toggle document.body overflow + padding compensation
  ModalContext.tsx (optional) -- for compound API: Modal.Header, Modal.Body, Modal.Footer
Rendered via createPortal into a #modal-root div appended to document.body.
stateModel:
isOpen is owned by the parent (controlled component) -- the modal itself holds no "am I open" state.
Internal-only state: a ref to the previously focused element (captured on open, restored on close) and a ref to the panel DOM node used for the focus trap query.
No global modal stack state needed unless supporting multiple simultaneous modals, in which case a small ModalManager context tracks an ordered array of open modal ids.
edgeCases: Modal opened by a button that unmounts before the modal closes (focus-return ref becomes stale/null -- fall back to body)
No focusable elements inside the modal at all (must still be able to Tab-trap on the panel itself via tabIndex=-1)
Nested modal opened from within a modal (confirm-delete inside edit-payment) -- focus trap must apply to the topmost one only
User clicks a native <select> that opens a browser-rendered dropdown -- must not be treated as an outside click
Async submit in progress: Escape and overlay click should be disabled until the request resolves
Very tall content requiring internal scroll while header/footer stay pinned
Rapid open/close toggling (double-clicking the trigger) should not leave focus-trap listeners duplicated
a11yChecklist: role="dialog" (or "alertdialog" for destructive confirmations) with aria-modal="true"
aria-labelledby pointing at the title element, aria-describedby for supporting text if present
Focus is programmatically moved to the panel or first focusable element on mount
All content outside the modal is hidden from assistive tech via aria-hidden or the inert attribute
Escape key and a labeled close button are both available -- never rely on overlay click alone
Focus is restored to the invoking element on close, not left on <body>
Color contrast of overlay text/panel meets WCAG AA even over busy background content
rubric:
Weak: renders inline (no portal), no focus trap, closes only via a close button, no Escape handling.
Solid: portal-based, Escape + overlay click close it, basic focus-trap via a hand-rolled Tab handler, returns focus on close.
Strong: correctly uses aria-modal + aria-hidden on siblings, handles the preventClose-while-submitting case, cleans up all listeners, avoids body-scroll layout shift.
Excellent: supports a compound-component API (Modal.Header/Body/Footer), handles nested modal stacking, and discusses using the native <dialog> element with showModal() as a lower-effort alternative and its trade-offs (default styling, backdrop pseudo-element, browser support).
interviewerQuestions: How would you support two modals open at once (e.g. a confirm dialog launched from within another modal)?
Why use a manual focus trap instead of the native <dialog> element -- what does showModal() give you for free, and what does it not?
How do you prevent the layout shift caused by the scrollbar disappearing when you lock body scroll?
How would you test the focus trap with React Testing Library / Playwright?
What happens to aria-hidden siblings if the modal is rendered via a portal outside the React root -- does your solution actually hide them?

title: Dropdown menu component (keyboard navigable, click-outside-to-close)
requirements:
Build a <DropdownMenu> for a table row's "..." actions menu (Edit, Duplicate, Archive, Delete) in an admin panel.
- Trigger button toggles menu open/closed
- Menu closes on: selecting an item, pressing Escape, clicking outside, or the trigger losing focus to something unrelated
- Full keyboard support: ArrowDown/ArrowUp move highlighted item, Enter/Space activates it, Home/End jump to first/last, typing a letter jumps to the next item starting with it
- Menu position flips above the trigger if there isn't enough viewport space below (basic collision handling)
- Supports disabled items and a visual separator between groups (e.g. separating "Delete" from safe actions)
- Menu content should not need to know about positioning logic -- keep it declarative
acceptanceCriteria: Opening the menu with keyboard (Enter/Space/ArrowDown on trigger) moves focus/highlight to the first enabled item
Clicking anywhere outside the trigger and menu closes it and returns focus to the trigger
Disabled items are skipped by arrow-key navigation and cannot be activated by click
Escape closes the menu and refocuses the trigger without triggering any item action
Menu never renders off-screen; it flips or shifts to stay within the viewport
Only one instance of a given dropdown is open at a time when rendered in a list (e.g. multiple table rows each with their own menu)
componentBreakdown:
DropdownMenu/
  DropdownMenu.tsx        -- root: owns open state, trigger ref, positions the panel
  DropdownMenuItem.tsx     -- individual item, handles disabled + typeahead registration
  useClickOutside.ts       -- hook: mousedown listener on document, checks ref containment
  useRovingIndex.ts        -- hook: manages highlighted index + keyboard handler
  usePopoverPosition.ts (optional) -- or use a library like Floating UI / Radix Popper for collision detection
In practice, most teams would reach for Radix UI's DropdownMenu primitive here -- worth mentioning that trade-off in the interview.
stateModel:
isOpen: boolean (local state in the root, or controlled by parent if multiple dropdowns need mutual exclusivity)
highlightedIndex: number, -1 when nothing is highlighted, reset to 0 (first enabled item) on open
Refs: triggerRef, menuRef (for click-outside and positioning), itemRefs array (for imperative .focus() calls, or use aria-activedescendant to avoid moving real DOM focus)
Typeahead buffer: a ref holding recently typed characters + a timeout id to reset it after ~500ms of inactivity
edgeCases: Menu triggered inside a scrollable table -- must reposition or close on scroll
Very long item labels causing menu overflow -- truncate with ellipsis + tooltip on hover
Rapid open of dropdown A while dropdown B is already open in the same row list -- B must close
Clicking a disabled item should visually show a not-allowed cursor and do nothing
Keyboard user tabs away mid-navigation (not via Escape) -- menu should still close
Menu content taller than viewport -- needs internal scroll with the trigger position preserved
Fast double Enter press should not fire the selected action twice
a11yChecklist: Trigger has aria-haspopup="menu" and aria-expanded reflecting open state
Menu container has role="menu"; items have role="menuitem" (or "menuitemcheckbox"/"menuitemradio" if applicable)
Use aria-activedescendant on the menu (keeping real focus on the trigger/menu container) OR move actual DOM focus to items -- pick one strategy consistently, do not mix
Disabled items carry aria-disabled="true" and are excluded from the accessible action but still readable
Typeahead matches item text via aria-label or textContent, not just visual label truncation
Focus returns to the trigger element when the menu closes by any means (Escape, selection, outside click)
rubric:
Weak: shows/hides menu with CSS only on hover or a single onClick toggle, no keyboard support, no outside-click handling.
Solid: click-outside works, Escape closes it, basic ArrowDown/Up navigation, focus returns to trigger.
Strong: full roving index with Home/End and typeahead, disabled items correctly skipped, viewport collision flipping.
Excellent: candidate recognizes this is exactly what Radix/Headless UI solve, implements it correctly by hand within time, and can articulate why a hand-rolled version is risky for production (subtle focus bugs, RTL, nested menus) vs. using a primitive.
interviewerQuestions: Why choose real DOM focus movement vs. aria-activedescendant here -- what are the trade-offs?
How would you make sure only one row menu is open at a time in a table with 100 rows, without keeping 100 pieces of open/close state?
How would you add submenus (nested menus opening on hover/ArrowRight)?
What would break if this menu were rendered inside a container with overflow: hidden -- how would you fix it?
Would you reach for Radix UI or Headless UI in production instead of this -- why or why not?

title: Tabs component (accessible, keyboard arrow navigation)
requirements:
Build a <Tabs> component for a settings page (Profile / Security / Billing / Notifications) in a SaaS app.
- Compound API: <Tabs><TabList><Tab/></TabList><TabPanels><TabPanel/></TabPanels></Tabs>
- Controlled and uncontrolled modes: accept activeTab + onChange, or defaultTab for internal state
- Arrow Left/Right (or Up/Down for a vertical variant) move between tabs; Home/End jump to first/last
- Tab activation can be "automatic" (focus moves the panel too) or "manual" (Enter/Space required to activate) -- support at least automatic
- Only the active tab panel is in the DOM's tab order / visible; inactive panels are hidden
- Disabled tabs are skippable via keyboard and visually distinct
acceptanceCriteria: Only one tab has tabIndex 0 at a time; the rest are -1 (roving tabindex pattern)
ArrowRight from the last tab wraps to the first (and ArrowLeft from first wraps to last)
Switching tabs by keyboard updates both the visually active tab and the associated panel content
Disabled tabs are never focused via arrow navigation and cannot be clicked into
Component works fully controlled (parent owns activeTab state) without any internal state fallback breaking
Deep-linking works: the active tab can be derived from a URL query param on mount
componentBreakdown:
Tabs/
  Tabs.tsx          -- context provider holding activeId + setActiveId, controlled/uncontrolled logic
  TabList.tsx        -- role="tablist", handles keydown for roving navigation
  Tab.tsx            -- role="tab", registers itself, reads active state from context
  TabPanel.tsx        -- role="tabpanel", only renders/shows when matching active id
  useControllableState.ts -- shared hook for the controlled/uncontrolled pattern, reused elsewhere (Accordion, etc.)
stateModel:
activeId: string, either controlled (prop + onChange callback) or uncontrolled (internal useState seeded by defaultTab).
Context value: { activeId, setActiveId, idPrefix } shared between TabList/Tab/TabPanel so they stay in sync without prop drilling.
No per-tab state beyond a stable id and disabled flag, both passed as props.
edgeCases: Tabs list overflowing horizontally on mobile -- needs scrollable tablist with visible active indicator
All tabs disabled except one -- keyboard nav must not infinite-loop trying to skip disabled entries
Programmatic activeTab change from outside (e.g. "Upgrade plan" button jumps user to Billing tab)
Panel content with async data that should only fetch when its tab becomes active (lazy mount)
Rapid arrow-key presses should not desync the visual highlight from the actual active panel
Browser back/forward when tab state is synced to the URL
a11yChecklist: TabList has role="tablist"; each Tab has role="tab", aria-selected, and aria-controls pointing to its panel id
Each TabPanel has role="tabpanel" and aria-labelledby pointing back to its tab id
Roving tabindex: active tab has tabIndex=0, all others tabIndex=-1, so Tab key exits the whole tablist in one hop
Arrow keys move focus AND (in automatic mode) selection; Home/End jump to first/last enabled tab
Disabled tabs get aria-disabled="true" and are excluded from arrow-key traversal
Panel content is reachable via Tab key from the active tab without extra stops
rubric:
Weak: renders tabs as plain buttons with onClick only, all panels use conditional && rendering with no ARIA roles.
Solid: correct ARIA roles/relationships, click switching works, basic controlled/uncontrolled support.
Strong: full roving tabindex keyboard nav with wraparound, disabled tab handling, context-based compound component API.
Excellent: adds lazy panel mounting, URL sync, and discusses automatic vs. manual activation trade-offs (manual is better for panels with expensive content).
interviewerQuestions: How would you lazy-load a panel's data only the first time its tab becomes active, and keep it mounted afterward?
How would you sync the active tab to a URL query param without fighting React Router / Next.js navigation?
What changes for a vertical tabs layout (e.g. a settings sidebar) in terms of keyboard bindings?
How would you animate the active-tab underline sliding between tabs without janky reflows?
How do automatic vs. manual activation models differ, and when would you pick manual?

title: Accordion component (single or multi-expand, animated height)
requirements:
Build an <Accordion> for an FAQ section / order-details breakdown (e.g. "Items", "Shipping", "Payment" collapsible sections in an order summary page).
- Prop to control mode: "single" (opening one closes others) or "multiple" (independent toggles)
- Each item has a header (button) and a panel; clicking the header toggles that panel
- Smooth height animation on expand/collapse (no abrupt show/hide, no layout jank)
- Support a defaultExpanded set of item ids and a controlled expandedIds + onChange API
- Keyboard: Enter/Space toggles the focused header; ArrowUp/Down move focus between headers
acceptanceCriteria: In "single" mode, expanding one item collapses any other open item automatically
In "multiple" mode, any number of items can be open simultaneously
Expand/collapse animates height smoothly using either measured scrollHeight transitions or CSS grid-template-rows trick -- not a hard display:none jump
Content with dynamically changing height (e.g. an image that loads after mount) does not get clipped after the animation settles
Component works both controlled (expandedIds + onChange from parent) and uncontrolled (internal state)
Arrow keys move focus between accordion headers without needing Tab
componentBreakdown:
Accordion/
  Accordion.tsx        -- context: mode, expandedIds, toggle(id)
  AccordionItem.tsx     -- wraps a Header+Panel pair, exposes item id to context
  AccordionHeader.tsx    -- role button, aria-expanded, keydown for arrow nav
  AccordionPanel.tsx     -- animated height container
  useAnimatedHeight.ts   -- hook measuring scrollHeight and transitioning max-height, or using the CSS grid rows="0fr"->"1fr" technique
stateModel:
expandedIds: Set<string> (multiple mode) or a single string | null (single mode), controlled or uncontrolled via the same pattern as Tabs.
Per-panel animation state is transient and lives in the DOM/CSS transition, not React state -- avoid storing "isAnimating" in state per item if it can be done via CSS.
Context value: { mode, expandedIds, toggle }.
edgeCases: Toggling an item while its previous expand animation is still running (interrupt cleanly, do not double-animate)
Panel content that includes async-loaded images/data changing its natural height mid-animation
All items collapsed by default vs. one expanded by default -- ensure aria-expanded is correct from first render
Very long panel content -- animate up to a reasonable max-height or use the fr-unit grid technique which avoids hardcoding max-height entirely
Nested accordions (an accordion panel containing another accordion) -- keydown handlers must not conflict
Reduced-motion user preference (prefers-reduced-motion) should disable the animation, not just make it instant-looking by accident
a11yChecklist: Header is a real <button> with aria-expanded and aria-controls pointing at its panel id
Panel has role="region" and aria-labelledby pointing back at its header id (only necessary when panel is always in DOM)
Collapsed panel content is hidden from both visual users and screen readers (use hidden attribute or aria-hidden plus removing from tab order), not just visually clipped
ArrowUp/ArrowDown move focus between headers; Home/End jump to first/last header
Respect prefers-reduced-motion by skipping the height transition
Focus is never lost when a panel collapses while a focused element was inside it -- move focus back to the header
rubric:
Weak: uses display:none/block toggling with no animation, no ARIA attributes, single boolean per item with no single/multiple mode support.
Solid: correct aria-expanded/aria-controls, basic height animation via measured scrollHeight, single/multiple modes both work.
Strong: animation handles dynamic content height changes gracefully, keyboard arrow navigation between headers, respects reduced motion.
Excellent: uses the CSS grid-template-rows 0fr/1fr technique (avoids JS measuring entirely, handles dynamic content perfectly), and discusses trade-offs vs. the measured-height approach.
interviewerQuestions: Why does the grid-template-rows 0fr/1fr technique handle dynamic content height better than measuring scrollHeight in JS?
How would you persist which sections are expanded across a page refresh (e.g. localStorage or URL state)?
How would nested accordions affect your keyboard event handling -- would ArrowDown in an inner accordion leak to the outer one?
How do you respect prefers-reduced-motion, and why does it matter for vestibular disorders?
If content lazy-loads images inside a panel after it is expanded, how do you avoid a jump when the image finishes loading?

title: Toast notification system (queue, auto-dismiss, stacking, types)
requirements:
Build a global toast system for an ERP app: any component can call toast.success("Invoice saved") or toast.error("Payment failed") from anywhere, without prop drilling.
- Types: success, error, warning, info -- each with distinct color/icon
- Toasts auto-dismiss after a configurable duration (default 4s), but pause the timer on hover/focus
- Multiple toasts stack vertically, newest on top (or bottom, configurable), with a max-visible cap and overflow collapsing into a "+3 more" indicator
- Manual dismiss via a close button
- Exposes an imperative API (toast.success/error/warning/info/dismiss) usable from event handlers, API callbacks, anywhere -- not just from within a React component via a hook
acceptanceCriteria: Calling toast.success(...) from a plain async function (e.g. inside an axios .then()) works without needing to be inside a React component
Hovering a toast pauses its auto-dismiss timer; moving the mouse away resumes it from where it left off (not restarting fully)
Toasts render via a portal so they float above all other UI including modals
Screen readers announce new toasts without needing the user to navigate to them
Dismissing a toast mid-enter-animation does not throw or leave orphaned DOM nodes
A rapid burst of 10 toasts in one tick does not crash or visually break the stack -- excess collapses or scrolls sensibly
componentBreakdown:
toast/
  ToastProvider.tsx     -- renders the portal + the visible stack, subscribes to the store
  toastStore.ts          -- plain module-level store (array of toasts + subscribers), NOT React context, so it works outside components
  useToastStore.ts        -- hook that subscribes a component (the ToastProvider) to store changes via useSyncExternalStore
  Toast.tsx              -- single toast visual: icon, message, close button, progress bar
  toast.ts               -- the exported imperative API: toast.success/error/warning/info/dismiss(id)
stateModel:
Lives outside React in a module-level store: { toasts: ToastItem[] }, with a Set of subscriber callbacks.
toast.success(msg) pushes a new ToastItem { id, type, message, duration, createdAt } and notifies subscribers.
ToastProvider uses useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.getSnapshot) to re-render whenever the store changes -- this is the key architectural choice since toast needs to be callable from non-component code.
Per-toast remaining-time tracking (for pause/resume) is kept in a ref map inside Toast, not in the global store, to avoid unnecessary global re-renders every animation frame.
edgeCases: toast.error called during server-side rendering (no window) -- must no-op or queue safely rather than crash
Component that called toast(...) unmounts before the toast auto-dismisses -- toast lifecycle must be independent of the calling component's lifecycle
Two identical error toasts fired in a tight loop (e.g. a retried failed request) -- consider de-duplication by message+type
User dismisses a toast exactly as its auto-dismiss timer fires (race between manual and automatic removal)
Toast stack pushed below the viewport on very small mobile screens
Very long message text needing truncation with a "show more" affordance instead of breaking the layout
Reduced motion preference disabling slide/fade animations
a11yChecklist: Toast container has aria-live="polite" (or "assertive" for error type) so screen readers announce new toasts automatically
Each toast is a role="status" (or role="alert" for errors) region
Close button has an accessible label ("Dismiss notification") and is keyboard reachable
Auto-dismiss timing gives users enough time to read -- pausing on focus-within (not just mouse hover) matters for keyboard/AT users
Do not rely on color alone to distinguish success/error/warning -- pair with distinct icons and text
Toasts must not steal focus from whatever the user was doing when they appear
rubric:
Weak: toast state lives in React context/useState, meaning it can only be triggered from inside components that have access to the provider, and duplicate/burst handling is not considered.
Solid: module-level store with a working imperative API, basic auto-dismiss and manual close, portal rendering.
Strong: pause-on-hover/focus with accurate remaining-time tracking, aria-live announcements, handles bursts and de-duplication.
Excellent: uses useSyncExternalStore correctly for the React/vanilla-JS bridge, discusses SSR safety, and designs a clean priority/queueing system (e.g. error toasts jump the max-visible cap ahead of info toasts).
interviewerQuestions: Why use useSyncExternalStore instead of React Context here -- what specifically breaks with Context for this use case?
How would you de-duplicate identical error toasts fired repeatedly by a retrying network request?
How would you prioritize an error toast so it is never hidden behind the max-visible cap while info toasts are?
How would this behave under React 18 Strict Mode double-invocation, and does your effect cleanup handle it?
How would you unit test the pause-on-hover timer logic without flaky real-time waits?

title: Search input with debounce
requirements:
Build a search box for a product catalog admin page that filters a list as the user types, without firing an API call on every keystroke.
- Debounce the search-triggering call by ~300-400ms after the user stops typing
- Show a loading indicator while a debounced search request is in flight
- Cancel/ignore stale responses if a newer request was fired after an older one that hasn't resolved yet (race condition)
- Clear button (X) resets the input and results immediately, bypassing the debounce
- Support both "debounce the API call" and being reusable for pure client-side filtering (debounce still helps avoid re-filtering a large array on every keystroke)
acceptanceCriteria: Typing quickly ("reac" then "react") results in exactly one network call for "react", not five
If a slow response for an earlier query resolves after a faster response for a later query, the UI shows the later query's results, not the stale earlier ones
Pressing the clear button resets input and results instantly with no debounce delay
Loading spinner appears only while a request tied to the current input value is pending
Unmounting the component while a debounced call is pending does not cause a "set state on unmounted component" warning
Debounce delay is configurable via a prop, not hardcoded inside the component
componentBreakdown:
SearchInput/
  SearchInput.tsx      -- controlled input + clear button + loading indicator
  useDebouncedValue.ts  -- generic hook: returns a debounced copy of a fast-changing value
  useSearchQuery.ts      -- hook combining the debounced value with a data-fetching call, handling race conditions (AbortController or a request-id ref)
Reusable useDebouncedValue can also back other features (filter panels, slider inputs that trigger recalculation).
stateModel:
rawValue: string -- updates on every keystroke, drives the input's visual value immediately (input must never feel laggy)
debouncedValue: string -- derived from rawValue via useDebouncedValue(rawValue, delay), only updates after the delay elapses with no further changes
Fetch state: isLoading/data/error, keyed off debouncedValue via a useEffect or a data-fetching library (React Query) -- avoid storing "isLoading" as a hand-rolled boolean if using React Query, since it manages that already.
A ref or AbortController per request to guard against out-of-order responses.
edgeCases: Empty query after clearing -- should reset to an initial "all items" or empty-state view, not show a spinner forever
User pastes a long string instantly (no gradual typing) -- debounce must still apply correctly
Backspacing to empty then retyping the same string rapidly
Network request that fails entirely (not just slow) while a newer one succeeds -- error should not overwrite valid newer data
Very fast typer whose keystrokes outpace the debounce window entirely (no debounce fires until they pause)
Component re-mounted with a different debounce delay prop mid-session
a11yChecklist: Input has an associated <label> (visually hidden if using placeholder-as-label pattern is avoided)
Loading state is announced via aria-busy or a visually-hidden aria-live region ("Searching...") without being disruptive on every keystroke
Clear button has an accessible label ("Clear search") and is keyboard reachable
Search results update is announced via aria-live="polite" once settled, not per-keystroke
Input retains focus throughout typing and after clearing
rubric:
Weak: uses setTimeout/clearTimeout ad hoc inside the component with no cleanup, no race-condition handling, debounces the input's visual value itself (making typing feel laggy).
Solid: extracts a reusable useDebouncedValue hook, debounces the derived search trigger (not the visible input), basic loading state.
Strong: handles out-of-order responses correctly (AbortController or request-id guard), proper effect cleanup, configurable delay.
Excellent: integrates cleanly with React Query/SWR (which handles caching, race conditions, and retries for free) and can explain when to still hand-roll debouncing (heavy client-side array filtering) vs. delegate to a data library (server queries).
interviewerQuestions: Why debounce the API call rather than the input's visible value -- what UX problem does that avoid?
How does the request-id ref pattern protect against out-of-order responses, and how would AbortController do the same job differently?
How would this change if you swapped in React Query -- what would you delete?
How would you unit test the debounce timing without making the test suite slow or flaky?
When would you use throttling instead of debouncing, and can you give an example from this same app?

title: Autocomplete/typeahead component (keyboard nav, highlighting matches, async suggestions)
requirements:
Build an autocomplete input for a "Add customer" form in a CRM, where typing a name fetches matching customers from an API and lets the user pick one (or free-type a new one).
- As the user types, fetch suggestions (debounced) and show a listbox below the input
- Matching substring within each suggestion is visually highlighted (bolded)
- Full keyboard support: ArrowDown/Up move through suggestions, Enter selects the highlighted one, Escape closes the list, typing again re-opens it
- Clicking a suggestion selects it and fills the input
- Loading, empty ("No customers found"), and error states inside the listbox
- Selecting a value fires an onSelect(customer) callback with the full object, not just the display string
acceptanceCriteria: ArrowDown from the input opens the list (if closed) and highlights the first suggestion; further ArrowDown moves through the list without wrapping past the last item into nothing
Enter with a highlighted suggestion selects it, fills the input with its display text, and closes the list
Enter with no highlighted suggestion (e.g. user is free-typing) submits the raw text as a "custom" value rather than doing nothing
Clicking outside the input/listbox closes the list without altering the current input text
The matched substring is highlighted case-insensitively even when the API returns mixed-case results
Rapid typing does not cause an older, slower response to override a newer, faster one in the displayed list
Screen reader users hear the number of results and the currently highlighted option
componentBreakdown:
Autocomplete/
  Autocomplete.tsx      -- input + listbox composition, owns open/highlighted/query state
  useDebouncedValue.ts   -- shared with the search-input challenge
  useSuggestions.ts       -- data-fetching hook (React Query useQuery keyed by debounced query), race-safe
  HighlightMatch.tsx      -- splits a label around the matched substring and wraps the match in <mark> or <strong>
  SuggestionListbox.tsx    -- role="listbox", renders loading/empty/error/list states
stateModel:
query: string (raw input value)
debouncedQuery: string
isOpen: boolean -- whether the listbox is visible
highlightedIndex: number, -1 meaning none highlighted
suggestions/isLoading/isError from a query hook keyed by debouncedQuery
selectedCustomer: the committed selection, lifted to the parent form via onSelect -- the component itself is otherwise uncontrolled for its internal query/open state.
edgeCases: User selects a suggestion, then edits the input again -- must re-open suggestions rather than keep showing the old selection's state
API returns zero results -- show a clear empty state, not a blank collapsed list that looks broken
API errors (network failure) -- show an inline retry affordance inside the listbox rather than silently failing
User tabs away mid-search -- pending debounce/fetch should not set state after the component context has moved on
Extremely fast typing outpacing debounce, then a paste event replacing the whole value at once
Duplicate suggestion labels for different underlying records (e.g. two customers both named "Alex Kim") -- selection must use id, not label, to disambiguate
Long suggestion lists needing virtualization for performance (100+ items)
a11yChecklist: Input has role="combobox", aria-autocomplete="list", aria-expanded, and aria-controls pointing to the listbox id
Listbox has role="listbox"; each suggestion has role="option" and a stable id used by aria-activedescendant on the input
aria-activedescendant on the input tracks the currently highlighted option so screen readers announce it without moving real focus off the input
A visually-hidden live region announces result count changes ("5 results available") after the debounce settles
Escape closes the listbox and returns to a clean input state without submitting a selection

Highlighted match text is conveyed by more than just bold styling for screen readers (it is redundant with the text itself, so this is mainly a visual/cognitive aid, not an aria concern) -- confirm contrast of the highlight is sufficient
rubric:
Weak: fetches on every keystroke with no debounce, no keyboard navigation, plain onClick-only selection, no ARIA roles at all.
Solid: debounced fetch, ArrowUp/Down + Enter/Escape work, basic role="listbox"/"option" markup, loading/empty states shown.
Strong: uses aria-activedescendant correctly (focus stays on input), handles race conditions, highlights matched substrings safely (no raw HTML injection), disambiguates by id not label.
Excellent: integrates with React Query for caching/race-safety, adds virtualization for large suggestion sets, and discusses how this differs from a native <datalist> (styling/keyboard control trade-offs) and when to just use one.
interviewerQuestions: Why use aria-activedescendant instead of moving real DOM focus into the listbox items?
The onBlur uses a setTimeout hack to let onMouseDown fire first -- why is that necessary, and is there a cleaner way?
How would you virtualize this list if the API could return hundreds of matches?
How would you support selecting a value that is NOT in the suggestion list (e.g. adding a brand-new customer inline)?
How does React Query's caching change your race-condition handling compared to a hand-rolled fetch + AbortController?

title: Data table component (columns, search, filters, sort, pagination, selection, a11y, responsive, URL sync)
requirements:
Design and build a reusable <DataTable<T>> for an admin panel listing orders in a marketplace (id, customer, status, total, createdAt, items count).
This is the flagship "build a real product primitive" exercise -- expect it to be scoped down live (interviewer will say "just do sort + pagination" or "skip virtualization, just describe it").
- Typed column definitions: Column<T> with key, header, accessor/render function, sortable flag, width, and an optional align
- A single reusable <DataTable data={rows} columns={columns} .../> that has zero knowledge of "orders" specifically -- must work for any entity shape T
- Text search across one or more searchable columns (client-side substring match, or a server search param)
- Multiple independent filters (e.g. status = shipped, dateRange = last 30 days) combinable with AND semantics
- Click a sortable column header to sort ascending; click again for descending; click again to clear sort (3-state cycle)
- Pagination controls (page number, next/prev, jump to page) plus a page-size selector (10/25/50/100)
- Loading skeleton rows while data is fetching, an error state with a Retry button, and an empty state ("No orders match your filters") distinct from the loading state
- Row selection: a header checkbox for select-all-on-page (tri-state: unchecked/checked/indeterminate), and per-row checkboxes, exposing selectedIds to the parent for bulk actions (e.g. "Export 12 selected")
- Responsive: below a breakpoint, the table degrades to a stacked card layout per row rather than horizontally scrolling an unreadable table
- Current search/filters/sort/page/pageSize are reflected in the URL query string so the view is bookmarkable/shareable and survives a refresh
- Explicitly discuss (in the design, verbally or in code comments) client-side vs. server-side pagination/sorting/filtering trade-offs, and how the component's public API needs to change to support server-side mode
- Mention virtualization (e.g. react-window / TanStack Virtual) as the answer for very large datasets, and why pagination is usually preferred over virtualization for typical admin tables
acceptanceCriteria: Column definitions are fully typed: Column<T> constrains accessor/render to keys that actually exist on T, so a typo in a column key is a compile error
Clicking a sortable header cycles asc -> desc -> none, updates the sort indicator icon, and re-sorts (or re-requests) data accordingly
Search + filters + sort all combine correctly -- e.g. searching "acme" while filtered to status=shipped and sorted by total desc shows the correct intersected, ordered subset
Changing page size resets to page 1 and does not silently drop the current filters

Selecting rows across a page change either persists selection across pages (documented choice) or explicitly clears it with a visible reason -- this must be a deliberate, stated decision, not an accident
Reloading the page (hard refresh) with a URL like ?search=acme&status=shipped&sort=total:desc&page=2 restores the exact same view
On a narrow viewport, the same data renders as readable stacked cards with labeled fields instead of a horizontally-scrolling table
Loading, error, and empty states are visually and semantically distinct, and error state offers a working Retry that re-issues the last request/filter combination
componentBreakdown:
DataTable/
  DataTable.tsx              -- top-level: composes toolbar, table/cards, pagination; owns no business logic about "orders"
  DataTableToolbar.tsx        -- search input + filter controls + bulk action bar (shown when selectedIds.length > 0)
  DataTableHeader.tsx          -- column headers, sort click handling, select-all checkbox (tri-state)
  DataTableRow.tsx / DataTableCard.tsx -- two render paths for the same row, chosen by a useMediaQuery breakpoint hook
  DataTablePagination.tsx       -- page controls + page-size select
  DataTableSkeleton.tsx         -- loading placeholder rows matching column widths
  useTableState.ts               -- central hook: reads/writes URL search params for search/filters/sort/page/pageSize, exposes a typed TableState + setters
  useTableData.ts (server mode)    -- React Query hook that takes TableState and returns { rows, total, isLoading, isError, refetch }
  types.ts                        -- Column<T>, SortState, TableState, DataTableProps<T>
edgeCases: Sorting by a column whose values are sometimes null/undefined (e.g. some orders have no assigned rep) -- define a stable ordering (nulls last)
Filter combination that yields zero rows -- show the empty state with an explicit "Clear filters" action, not just "No data"
Selecting all on page 1, then navigating to page 2 -- decide and clearly surface whether selection is per-page or global across pages
Extremely large dataset (50k+ rows) in client-side mode -- discuss why this should push you toward server-side mode or virtualization, not just "make client-side faster"

Server-side mode: a request for page 5 while filters changed mid-flight returns stale results for the old filter set -- needs request cancellation/de-duplication (same race-condition pattern as the search/autocomplete challenges)
Page number in the URL exceeds total pages after a filter shrinks the result set -- must clamp back to a valid page rather than showing a blank page
Two sortable columns of different types (string vs. number vs. date) -- comparator must be type-aware, not a naive string comparison that breaks numeric/date ordering

Column with a custom render function (e.g. a status badge) that is not directly sortable/searchable by its rendered output -- sorting/search must operate on the underlying raw value, not the rendered JSX
a11yChecklist: Table has a caption or aria-label describing its content ("Orders, filtered by status: shipped, sorted by total descending")
Sortable column headers are buttons with aria-sort ("ascending"/"descending"/"none") on the parent <th>, and the sort action is reachable and operable via keyboard (Enter/Space), not click-only

Row/select-all checkboxes have clear accessible labels ("Select row for order #1042", "Select all orders on this page") and the select-all checkbox correctly exposes its indeterminate state to assistive tech
Roving tabindex or logical tab order lets keyboard users move through interactive cells (checkbox, row actions) without an excessive number of Tab stops per row
Loading state is announced via aria-busy on the table region; error and empty states use role="status"/role="alert" appropriately so screen reader users are not left staring at a silently empty table
Pagination controls have clear accessible names ("Go to page 3", "Next page") and the current page is indicated via aria-current="page"
The responsive card layout preserves the same semantic labeling per field (e.g. "Status: Shipped") so information is not lost for screen reader users when the table visually collapses
rubric:
Weak: single hardcoded table for "orders" with inline JSX per column, no types, sorting/filtering done with ad hoc component state that resets unpredictably, no accessibility attributes, no responsive behavior.
Solid: generic Column<T> config drives rendering, client-side search/filter/sort/pagination pipeline works correctly and is memoized, basic loading/error/empty states, checkbox selection with a header select-all (even if not perfectly tri-state).
Strong: full typed Column<T>/TableState API supporting both client- and server-side modes behind the same interface, correct tri-state select-all with indeterminate, proper aria-sort/table semantics, a working responsive card fallback, URL-synced state that survives refresh.
Excellent: candidate proactively discusses when to flip from client- to server-side (dataset size, filter complexity, need for cross-page aggregate stats), mentions virtualization as the alternative to pagination for huge in-memory lists and explains why pagination is usually still preferred in admin UIs (predictable performance, easier "which page am I on" mental model, works with server-side truly-huge datasets where virtualization alone doesn't help), and explicitly calls out that filters must ALSO be validated/enforced server-side (a user could hand-craft query params to request data outside their permission scope) -- client-side filtering is a UX convenience, never a security boundary.
interviewerQuestions: How would this component's public API change to support server-side filtering/sorting/pagination instead of client-side -- what props come out, what comes in?
Your select-all checkbox is per-page. How would you support a global "select all 4,000 matching rows" action, and what would the bulk-action confirmation UI need to say?
Why store TableState in the URL instead of component state -- what specific user scenarios does that fix?
How do you sort a column whose display value is a rendered badge (e.g. status) by its underlying raw value instead of the rendered JSX?
At what row count would you reach for virtualization over pagination, and why do most production admin tables still choose pagination?
A user edits the URL query string directly to request status=internal_only which their role should not see -- what breaks, and whose job is it to prevent that?

title: Client-side pagination component
requirements:
Build a standalone <Pagination> control (decoupled from any specific table) for a product listing page with a known, already-in-memory array of items.
- Props: totalItems, pageSize, currentPage, onPageChange
- Renders page number buttons with ellipsis collapsing for large page counts (e.g. 1 2 3 ... 8 9 10, not 40 buttons)
- Prev/Next buttons disabled appropriately at the first/last page
- A "Go to page" input for jumping directly (optional but a nice-to-have)
- Fully controlled component -- it renders nothing about the data itself, only page-selection UI
acceptanceCriteria: Prev is disabled on page 1, Next is disabled on the last page
Ellipsis collapsing shows the current page with a window of neighbors plus first/last page, not every page number when there are e.g. 50 pages
Clicking a page number calls onPageChange with the correct 1-indexed page number
Changing pageSize externally recalculates total pages and clamps currentPage if it now exceeds the new total
Component renders nothing (or is disabled) gracefully when totalItems is 0
Keyboard users can Tab through page buttons and activate them with Enter/Space; the current page is not a dead end for focus
componentBreakdown:
Pagination/
  Pagination.tsx        -- computes visible page numbers (with ellipsis) and renders buttons
  usePaginationRange.ts   -- pure function/hook: (currentPage, totalPages, siblingCount) -> (number | 'ellipsis')[]
  PageSizeSelect.tsx (optional) -- separate small component for the 10/25/50/100 dropdown, composed alongside Pagination
stateModel: Fully controlled by the parent: currentPage and pageSize are props, not internal state. The component computes totalPages = Math.ceil(totalItems / pageSize) and the visible page-number window as a pure derived value (useMemo), with zero internal state of its own beyond perhaps a transient "go to page" input's typed value before submission.
edgeCases: totalItems = 0 (no pages at all)
Only 1 page total -- prev/next and page buttons should not render or should all be disabled

currentPage passed in from the parent that is out of range (e.g. stale prop after a filter shrinks the result set) -- component should not crash, and should signal/clamp rather than silently render an invalid state
Very large totalItems (e.g. 100,000 rows / small pageSize = thousands of pages) -- ellipsis logic must still produce a small, bounded number of buttons
Rapid clicking Next repeatedly near the last page boundary
"Go to page" input receiving non-numeric input or a number outside the valid range
a11yChecklist: Root element has role="navigation" and aria-label="Pagination"
The current page button has aria-current="page"
Prev/Next buttons have descriptive aria-labels ("Previous page", "Next page"), not just chevron icons with no text alternative
Disabled Prev/Next use the disabled attribute (not just a visual style) so keyboard/AT users get correct semantics
Ellipsis is marked aria-hidden (it is decorative, not an interactive element) and does not receive focus
rubric:
Weak: renders a button per page with no ellipsis collapsing (breaks visually past ~15 pages), no disabled-state handling, no ARIA.
Solid: correct prev/next disabling, ellipsis collapsing works for typical cases, aria-current present.
Strong: pure, well-tested usePaginationRange logic handling all edge counts (0, 1, few, many pages) correctly, clamps out-of-range currentPage, fully keyboard operable.
Excellent: also supports a "Go to page" input with validation, and discusses when to swap this component for cursor-based (next/prev token) pagination instead of page-number based, which matters once the data source moves server-side.
interviewerQuestions: How does your ellipsis-collapsing logic behave at the boundaries -- page 1, page 2, second-to-last page, last page?
What would you change about this component's API to support server-side pagination where you do not know totalItems until the first response arrives?
When would you use cursor-based pagination (next/prev opaque tokens) instead of page-number pagination, and what does that do to this component's props?
How would you test usePaginationRange thoroughly given how many boundary cases it has?
How do you keep this component reusable across a product list, an order history table, and a search-results page with different total counts and page sizes?

title: Server-side pagination design (API contract and UI, design-level)
requirements:
This is a design-and-discuss round more than a pure coding round: design how a large orders table (millions of rows) in an ERP backend should be paginated end-to-end, then sketch the supporting UI states.
- Propose an API contract: request shape (page/pageSize vs. cursor-based) and response shape (rows, total or hasMore, and why)
- Explain why offset-based pagination (LIMIT/OFFSET or page=N) degrades at scale (deep offset scans) and where cursor/keyset pagination (WHERE created_at < :cursor ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT :n) is preferable
- Design how sorting and filtering interact with the chosen pagination strategy (cursor pagination gets significantly harder when sort column can change)
- Design the loading UX for page transitions: skeleton vs. keep-previous-data-visible-while-fetching (avoid a jarring blank flash)
- Discuss caching strategy on the client (React Query keepPreviousData / placeholderData, or Suspense) so navigating back to a previously seen page is instant
- Address total-count cost: getting an exact COUNT(*) on a huge table is expensive -- discuss approximate counts, "many more" indicators instead of exact totals, or count-on-demand
acceptanceCriteria: Candidate can articulate concretely why OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 25 is slow on a large table and what keyset/cursor pagination does differently
Candidate proposes a concrete response shape (e.g. { data: T[], pageInfo: { nextCursor: string | null, hasMore: boolean } }) rather than hand-waving
Candidate identifies that cursor pagination requires a stable, unique sort key (often a composite of the sort column + id as a tiebreaker) to avoid skipped/duplicated rows when values tie
Candidate addresses what happens to "jump to page 47" UX under cursor pagination (generally not supported directly -- discuss trade-off vs. offset pagination which does support arbitrary page jumps)
Candidate proposes a concrete client-side loading UX (e.g. React Query keepPreviousData) that avoids a full-page loading flash on page change
Candidate flags that exact COUNT(*) at scale is a real cost and proposes a mitigation (cached/approximate count, capped "1000+" style indicator, or count only fetched lazily)
componentBreakdown:
Even though this is design-heavy, sketch the pieces:
API layer: GET /orders?cursor=...&limit=25&sort=createdAt:desc&status=shipped -> { data, pageInfo: { nextCursor, hasMore } }
Client:
  useOrdersQuery.ts -- React Query useInfiniteQuery or useQuery keyed by { cursor, filters, sort }, with placeholderData: keepPreviousData
  OrdersTable.tsx -- renders rows + a "Load more" or Next-only pagination control (no direct page-N jump in pure cursor mode)
  OrdersTableHybrid.tsx (if hybrid) -- offers page-N jump backed by a server that still uses keyset internally but exposes an offset-like index for convenience, accepting the performance trade-off only within a bounded page-count window
stateModel:
Client holds: { cursorStack: string[] (to support "Prev" by remembering prior cursors), filters, sort }.
Because cursor pagination has no cheap "go back 3 pages," the client must remember the cursor used to reach each page it has visited (a stack), popping it to go back, rather than recomputing an offset.
Server holds no session state -- cursors are opaque, stable tokens (often base64-encoded {sortValue, id}) that the server can decode and resume from statelessly.
edgeCases: Sort column changes mid-session -- any remembered cursors for the old sort order are invalid and must be discarded, resetting to the first page
A row that was the cursor boundary gets deleted between requests -- the server must degrade gracefully (skip to the next valid row) rather than erroring
Ties in the sort column (e.g. two orders with the exact same createdAt timestamp) -- composite cursor (createdAt, id) needed to avoid dropping or duplicating rows across pages
User wants to jump directly to "page 50" -- explicitly not supported by pure cursor pagination; document this as a deliberate product trade-off or offer a hybrid approach
Filter change while viewing page 3 -- must reset the cursor stack, not attempt to keep the old cursor against a new filtered result set
Real-time inserts (new orders arriving) shifting a naive offset-based view -- cursor pagination is naturally more stable here since it anchors to a value, not a position
a11yChecklist: Announce page/result-set changes via an aria-live region ("Showing orders 26-50") even though there is no numbered page button to carry that context
Next/Prev (or Load more) controls have clear accessible names and reflect disabled state when hasMore is false
Loading-more state (e.g. infinite scroll variant) is announced so screen reader users know new content is being fetched, not that the list has silently ended
If offering a hybrid page-jump input, validate and announce invalid page requests clearly
rubric:
Weak: candidate assumes page=N/pageSize is fine at any scale, has no answer for why deep pagination is slow, and does not distinguish client caching from the pagination strategy itself.
Solid: candidate can explain offset vs. cursor pagination conceptually and picks one appropriately for the stated scale.
Strong: candidate designs a concrete API contract with an opaque composite cursor, addresses the tie-breaking and filter/sort-change invalidation issues, and proposes keepPreviousData-style UX.
Excellent: candidate discusses hybrid strategies used in real products (e.g. keyset pagination under the hood exposed as a bounded page-jump for the first N pages only, "load more" beyond that), the approximate-count problem and its mitigations, and ties the discussion back to how the UI component's public API and loading states change to support this.
referenceSolution:
Design write-up (talking points to hit, not literal code to type):

1. API contract: cursor-based, e.g. GET /orders?cursor=<opaque>&limit=25&sort=createdAt:desc plus filter params. Response: { data, pageInfo: { nextCursor, hasMore } }. The cursor encodes the composite key (sortColumnValue, id) so ties are broken deterministically -- e.g. base64 of { createdAt: '2026-01-02T10:00:00Z', id: 'ord_456' }.

2. Why not OFFSET/LIMIT at scale: 'SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 25 OFFSET 500000' still has to scan/skip 500,000 rows in most engines before returning the page -- cost grows linearly with page depth. Keyset pagination instead does 'WHERE (created_at, id) < (:lastCreatedAt, :lastId) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 25', which uses an index seek regardless of how deep the user has paged.

3. Sorting/filtering interaction: any change to the sort column or filter set invalidates existing cursors (they were computed against a different ordering/subset), so the client must reset to page 1 (drop cursorStack) whenever sort or filters change -- exactly like the resetting-page-to-1 rule in the DataTable challenge.

4. 'Jump to page 47' trade-off: pure cursor pagination cannot do this cheaply (no concept of absolute position). If the product genuinely needs arbitrary page jumps at scale, either (a) accept OFFSET-based pagination but cap how deep users can go (e.g. only expose the first 100 pages, forcing filtering instead of endless browsing), or (b) offer cursor pagination as the default 'Next/Load more' experience and treat deep jump as a rare, explicitly slower operation.

5. Client loading UX: use React Query's placeholderData: keepPreviousData (v4/v5) so the previous page's rows stay visible (dimmed/disabled) while the next page loads, instead of unmounting to a skeleton and causing a jarring flash; combine with a small inline spinner near the pagination control rather than a full-table skeleton on every page change.

6. Total count cost: avoid SELECT COUNT(*) on every request for a huge table -- options: (a) show 'hasMore' boolean only, no total; (b) show an approximate count from a periodically-refreshed materialized stat or the database's query planner estimate; (c) cap an exact count query at e.g. 1,000 with a 'LIMIT 1000' trick and display '1000+ results' beyond that threshold, only computing the real count on explicit user request (e.g. clicking 'show exact count').

7. Real-time stability: because cursor pagination anchors to a value rather than a row position, new inserts (e.g. a fresh order arriving) do not shift already-fetched pages the way OFFSET-based pagination would (which can show the same row twice or skip one as rows shift position) -- worth calling out as an added benefit for a live-updating admin table.
interviewerQuestions: How do you handle a request whose cursor points to a row that has since been deleted?
What happens to your cursor scheme if the sort direction is user-toggleable between asc and desc on the same column?
How would you support both "Load more" (cursor) and "Jump to page N" (offset) in the same product without contradicting each other?
How would you validate/reject a tampered or malformed cursor value coming from the client?
How does this design change if the "orders" data actually lived across multiple shards or services rather than one SQL table?

title: Search + filtering + sorting combined pipeline UI
requirements:
Build the filter/sort/search toolbar and results pipeline for a marketplace listings page (like an internal Etsy/Airbnb admin view): a search box, a multi-select category filter, a price-range filter, a status toggle, and a sort dropdown, all combining over one in-memory dataset.
- Text search matches title/description substrings, case-insensitive
- Category filter is multi-select (OR within the category filter, AND against other filters)
- Price range filter is a min/max pair
- Status filter is a single-select segmented control (all/active/draft/archived)
- Sort dropdown: newest, price-low-high, price-high-low, most-popular
- All filters combine correctly (AND across filter types, OR within a multi-select's own options)
- A visible "results count" and a "Clear all filters" action that appears only when at least one filter/search/sort deviates from defaults
acceptanceCriteria: Selecting 2 categories shows listings matching EITHER category (OR), while also respecting the price range and status filters applied simultaneously (AND)
Combining a search term with filters that together produce zero results shows a clear empty state with a one-click "Clear all filters"
Sort order is stable and correctly reapplied whenever the underlying filtered set changes (e.g. adding a filter does not reset sort to default)
Price min > max is either prevented in the UI or clearly flagged as invalid rather than silently producing wrong results
The whole pipeline (filter -> search -> sort) is a pure derived computation (useMemo) recalculated only when the dataset or the filter/search/sort state actually changes, not on unrelated re-renders
Filter/search/sort state is shareable via URL (same pattern as the data table challenge) so a filtered view can be bookmarked
componentBreakdown:
ListingsExplorer/
  FilterToolbar.tsx        -- search input + category multiselect + price range + status segmented control + sort select
  useListingsFilters.ts     -- URL-synced state (search/categories/priceRange/status/sort), same pattern as useTableState
  useFilteredListings.ts     -- pure pipeline: applyFilters -> applySearch -> applySort, memoized
  ResultsSummaryBar.tsx      -- "128 results" + active filter chips + Clear all
  ListingsGrid.tsx           -- renders the final computed list
edgeCases: No categories selected should mean "match any category" (do not accidentally treat an empty multi-select as "match nothing")
Price filter with only min or only max set (open-ended range)
Non-numeric input typed into price fields
Search term matches a listing whose category/status/price would otherwise be filtered out -- filters and search combine with AND overall, so it correctly stays hidden
Very large active-filter chip list wrapping to multiple lines in the toolbar on smaller viewports
User rapidly toggles a filter checkbox multiple times -- final state must reflect the last real user intent, no stale closures from async handlers
a11yChecklist: Multi-select category filter is operable via checkboxes with clear labels, not just clickable divs, and communicates selected count
Price range inputs have associated labels ("Minimum price", "Maximum price") and appropriate inputmode/type="number"
Segmented status control uses radio-group semantics (role="radiogroup" with role="radio" children, or native radio inputs) so only one is selectable and it is announced correctly
Active filter chips have an accessible remove action per chip ("Remove filter: Category = Home Goods")
Results count change is announced via aria-live="polite" after filters settle, not on every keystroke
Sort dropdown is a real <select> or a fully keyboard-operable custom listbox with a clear label ("Sort by")
rubric:
Weak: each filter is wired directly to array mutation with .filter() chains scattered inline in the render function, no memoization, sort/filter state not shareable or resettable cleanly.
Solid: single FilterState object, filters combine correctly with AND/OR semantics as specified, memoized pipeline, working Clear all.
Strong: URL-synced state, active filter chips with individual removal, correct handling of open-ended price ranges and empty-category-means-all.
Excellent: candidate generalizes this into the same reusable state-sync hook used by the DataTable challenge, discusses moving the pipeline server-side once dataset size or filter complexity grows (faceted counts per filter option, which are expensive to compute purely client-side), and considers debouncing the price range/search inputs to avoid recomputing on every keystroke.
interviewerQuestions: How would you compute per-option facet counts (e.g. "Home Goods (34)") next to each category checkbox without recomputing the entire pipeline for every option on every render?
At what dataset size or filter complexity would you move this filtering logic server-side, and what would the API contract look like?
How would you debounce the price range inputs so the pipeline does not recompute on every keystroke while still feeling responsive?
How do "clear all" and "remove one filter chip" differ in implementation, and how do you avoid duplicating the reset logic?
How would this state model change if search needed to hit a server (fuzzy/typo-tolerant search) while categories/price/status stayed client-side?

title: Multi-step form (wizard with step validation and back/next)
requirements:
Build a 4-step onboarding wizard for a payments platform merchant signup: Step 1 Business Info, Step 2 Contact Details, Step 3 Bank Account, Step 4 Review & Submit.
- A visible step indicator (progress bar or numbered steps) showing current/completed/upcoming steps
- Next button validates only the current step's fields before advancing; Back always works without re-validating
- Data persists across steps (going back and forward does not lose what was typed)
- Final Review step shows a read-only summary of everything entered, with an "Edit" link per section that jumps back to the relevant step
- Submitting the whole form only happens on the last step, sending the combined payload once
- Refreshing the browser mid-wizard should not silently lose all progress (discuss/implement persistence, e.g. sessionStorage draft)
acceptanceCriteria: Clicking Next on a step with invalid fields shows field-level errors and does NOT advance to the next step
Clicking Back never triggers validation errors for the step being left, even if it currently has invalid data
Data entered in step 1, after navigating to step 3 and back to step 1, is still present and editable

The step indicator accurately reflects which steps are completed, current, and not yet visited, and (if allowed) lets users jump backward to a completed step by clicking it, but not forward past the current step
The final submit button is disabled (or shows a clear reason) if any earlier step somehow holds invalid data (e.g. via direct URL navigation to the review step)
A submission failure (e.g. server rejects the bank account) surfaces an error without discarding any of the entered data, and ideally routes the user back to the relevant step
Sensitive fields like a bank account number are masked in the UI and never logged to the console/analytics in plaintext
componentBreakdown:
MerchantOnboardingWizard/
  WizardProvider.tsx     -- React Hook Form instance spanning ALL steps (one form, not four separate forms), plus currentStep state
  StepIndicator.tsx        -- visual progress, clickable for completed steps only
  steps/BusinessInfoStep.tsx
  steps/ContactDetailsStep.tsx
  steps/BankAccountStep.tsx
  steps/ReviewStep.tsx
  useWizardNavigation.ts    -- next()/back()/goToStep(), gates next() behind trigger() (RHF's per-field-set validation)
  useDraftPersistence.ts     -- syncs form values to sessionStorage on change, restores on mount, clears on successful submit
stateModel:
One React Hook Form instance (useForm) holds the ENTIRE multi-step payload in a single form state object -- this avoids the classic bug of separate per-step state that has to be manually merged and re-synced.
currentStepIndex: number -- separate, simple useState, not part of the form state itself.
completedSteps: Set<number> -- tracks which steps have passed validation at least once, driving the step indicator and whether clicking a step number is allowed.
Validation is scoped per step via RHF's trigger(['field1','field2']) called with only the current step's field names, so earlier/later steps' errors do not block navigation.
Draft persistence: form values watched via useEffect + form.watch(), debounced, written to sessionStorage; on mount, defaultValues are seeded by reading that draft back (falling back to empty defaults if none exists).
edgeCases: User is on step 3, opens a new tab to the same URL -- should not silently share/overwrite state in a confusing way (discuss: sessionStorage is per-tab, which is usually correct here)
Validation schema for step 2 depends on an answer from step 1 (e.g. "business type" affects which fields are required later) -- cross-step conditional validation
User clicks a step number in the indicator to jump directly to a not-yet-validated future step -- must be prevented (only completed steps or the current step are reachable)
Submit request fails partway (e.g. timeout) -- must not clear the draft, must allow retry without re-entering everything
Browser back/forward button used instead of the wizard's own Back/Next -- should not desync the visual step indicator from the actual current step

Extremely long-lived draft in sessionStorage containing since-changed sensitive data (e.g. a bank number) -- discuss clearing it aggressively on submit/cancel and never persisting raw bank details in localStorage (which outlives the tab)
a11yChecklist: Step indicator conveys current step via aria-current="step", and each reachable step is a real button/link, not a bare div with onClick
Field-level validation errors are associated to their inputs via aria-describedby and announced (role="alert" or an aria-live region) when Next is blocked

Focus moves to the first invalid field (or the step heading) when validation fails on Next, and to the new step's heading when navigation succeeds, so keyboard/screen-reader users are not left with stale focus on a removed element
The overall multi-step form is understandable out of visual order -- e.g. announcing "Step 2 of 4: Contact Details" via a visually-hidden live region on step change
Back and Next buttons have unambiguous labels beyond just icons ("Back", "Continue")
Masked sensitive fields (bank account) still expose a way to reveal/verify input (e.g. a "show" toggle) that is itself keyboard accessible
rubric:
Weak: four separate uncontrolled forms/state objects per step manually stitched together, validation runs (or does not run) inconsistently, going back loses data.
Solid: single shared form state across steps, per-step validation gating Next, Back always allowed, data persists across navigation.
Strong: step indicator correctly reflects completed/current/locked-future steps, focus management on step change, a working Review step with per-section edit links.
Excellent: adds sessionStorage draft persistence with sensible security discussion around not persisting raw bank details insecurely, handles cross-step conditional validation, and explicitly notes that client-side validation here is a UX layer only -- the actual bank account and business verification MUST be re-validated server-side (e.g. via a payments KYC provider) since a modified client payload cannot be trusted for anything security- or compliance-sensitive.
interviewerQuestions: Why keep one React Hook Form instance across all steps instead of four independent ones -- what specific bug does that avoid?
How do you handle a validation rule in a later step that depends on a value chosen in an earlier step (e.g. business type affecting required fields)?
Where exactly does bank account data get persisted, and why is sessionStorage a safer default than localStorage here -- and what would you tell a PM who wants it to survive a closed tab?
How would the browser back/forward buttons interact with your wizard's step state if you also synced steps to the URL?
What server-side validation absolutely must happen regardless of what the client already validated, and why?

title: Form validation (React Hook Form + Zod style, realistic signup/checkout form)
requirements:
Build a checkout billing form for an e-commerce app: name, email, card holder name, card number, expiry, CVC, billing address (street/city/postal/country), and a "save card for later" checkbox.
- Use React Hook Form for form state and Zod for schema validation, connected via zodResolver
- Field-level error messages appear on blur (not aggressively on every keystroke) and clear as soon as the field becomes valid
- Cross-field validation: postal code format depends on the selected country
- Card number gets formatted with spaces every 4 digits as the user types, and validated with a Luhn checksum
- Submit button is disabled while the form is invalid or currently submitting, and shows a loading state during submission
- On successful submit, show a success state; on a server-side rejection (e.g. card declined), surface the specific server error against the right field or as a form-level banner
acceptanceCriteria: Submitting with any required field empty shows all relevant field errors at once and does not call the submit handler
An invalid email format shows an inline error only after the user leaves the field (blur) or attempts submit, not while they are still mid-typing on first pass
Card number input auto-formats with spaces (4242 4242 4242 4242) and rejects a number that fails the Luhn check with a clear message
Changing country from US to a country with a different postal code pattern re-validates the postal code field against the new rule immediately
A server-side error (e.g. "Card declined") returned from the submit call is displayed without needing a page reload, and does not clobber other valid field values
Submit button is disabled during submission (isSubmitting) so a double-click cannot fire two charge requests
componentBreakdown:
CheckoutForm/
  CheckoutForm.tsx      -- useForm + zodResolver, field layout, submit handling
  checkoutSchema.ts       -- zod schema, including the .superRefine for country-dependent postal code and the Luhn check
  CardNumberInput.tsx      -- controlled input with format-as-you-type logic wired through RHF's Controller
  FormField.tsx            -- small wrapper: label + input + error message, reused across all fields for consistent a11y wiring
  useSubmitCheckout.ts      -- mutation hook (e.g. React Query useMutation) mapping server error shapes back onto RHF's setError
stateModel:
All field values and validation state live inside React Hook Form's internal form state (register/Controller-driven), not duplicated into component useState.
mode: 'onBlur' (or 'onTouched') for the initial validation trigger, with reValidateMode: 'onChange' so a field that showed an error clears it as soon as it becomes valid on subsequent keystrokes -- this combination gives the "not aggressive on first pass, but responsive once an error is shown" behavior.
Submission state: formState.isSubmitting drives the disabled/loading button; server-side field errors are pushed into the same form state via setError('cardNumber', { message }) so they render through the same FormField error UI as client-side ones.
edgeCases: Pasting a card number that already includes spaces/dashes -- formatting logic must normalize before re-formatting, not double up separators
Country changed after postal code was already filled and valid for the old country -- must re-run validation against the new schema branch, not leave a stale "valid" state
Server rejects the card with a reason not mapped to any known field (e.g. a generic gateway timeout) -- must show a form-level banner rather than trying to force it onto a specific field
User is offline / request throws a network error rather than returning a structured API error -- distinct message from a card decline
Autofill from the browser filling multiple fields at once -- RHF/Zod validation should still run correctly on the autofilled values
CVC field length differs by card type (3 digits typical, 4 for some card networks) -- validation should not hardcode a single fixed length incorrectly
Rapid submit-button clicking before isSubmitting flips to true on the very first click (should still only fire one request)
a11yChecklist: Every input has a programmatically associated <label>, and errors are linked via aria-describedby, with aria-invalid toggled on the field
Field errors are in a live region or associated closely enough that screen reader users hear them without extra navigation (commonly role="alert" on the error text itself)
Card number input remains operable by screen readers/keyboard despite the formatting-as-you-type behavior (do not fight cursor position on every keystroke)
Submit button communicates its busy/disabled state via aria-busy or a visually-hidden "Submitting..." label, not color alone
Server-side/form-level error banner uses role="alert" so it is announced immediately, and receives focus or is placed where focus will naturally land next
Autofill and password-manager compatibility is not broken by overly aggressive custom input handling (e.g. do not block paste)
rubric:
Weak: manual useState per field with hand-rolled validation functions and no schema, error messages appear on every keystroke from the start (annoying UX), no card formatting or Luhn check.
