Solid: React Hook Form + Zod wired correctly via zodResolver, sensible onBlur/onChange revalidation strategy, basic required/format validation for all fields.
Strong: correct cross-field (country-dependent postal code) validation via superRefine, working card-number formatting + Luhn check, server errors mapped cleanly onto setError.
Excellent: candidate explicitly states that all of this client-side validation is a UX layer only -- the actual charge, card verification, and fraud checks must happen server-side/at the payment processor, and reiterates that raw card data ideally never touches the merchant's own backend at all (e.g. tokenized via Stripe Elements/PCI-compliant iframe) rather than being collected in a plain controlled input in a real production system.
interviewerQuestions: Why choose onBlur + reValidateMode onChange instead of just mode: onChange for the whole form -- what UX problem does that solve?
In a real production checkout, would you ever collect a raw card number in your own controlled input like this? What would you use instead, and why?
How do you map a structured server validation error response onto the right form field reliably, given the server and client might use slightly different field names?
How would you test the Luhn validation and the country-dependent postal code rule without hitting a real payment gateway?
How would you prevent the user from submitting the form twice if they click Pay, then click it again before isSubmitting flips?

title: Infinite scroll list (IntersectionObserver based)
requirements:
Build an infinite-scrolling activity feed for a social/marketplace app (e.g. "recent orders" or "activity log") that loads the next page of items automatically as the user nears the bottom, instead of using pagination buttons.
- Fetch page 1 on mount; fetch subsequent pages automatically when a sentinel element near the bottom of the list becomes visible
- Use IntersectionObserver (not a scroll event listener) to detect when to fetch the next page
- Show a loading spinner at the bottom while fetching the next page, and stop observing once there are no more pages (hasMore = false)
- Handle a failed page fetch with a retry affordance, without losing already-loaded items above it
- Avoid firing duplicate requests if the sentinel intersects again while a fetch is already in flight
acceptanceCriteria: Scrolling down triggers exactly one fetch per additional page, never a duplicate/parallel fetch for the same page
Reaching the last page (hasMore = false) stops observing the sentinel and removes or hides the loading spinner, replaced by an "You have reached the end" message
A failed page request shows a retry button at the bottom without clearing previously loaded items
Fast scrolling past the sentinel does not skip triggering a fetch (observer margin/threshold tuned so the fetch starts before the user physically hits the bottom)
The component correctly cleans up the IntersectionObserver on unmount (no memory leaks / errors calling setState after unmount)
List remains scroll-position-stable when new items are appended (no jump/flash at the append point)
componentBreakdown:
ActivityFeed/
  ActivityFeed.tsx        -- renders items + sentinel + loading/error/end states
  useInfiniteFeed.ts        -- wraps React Query's useInfiniteQuery (or a hand-rolled equivalent) exposing items, fetchNextPage, hasNextPage, isFetchingNextPage, isError
  useIntersectionObserver.ts -- generic hook: (ref, options) -> isIntersecting boolean, reused anywhere lazy-loading-on-visibility is needed (e.g. lazy images too)
  Sentinel.tsx              -- a near-invisible div rendered after the last item, observed for intersection
stateModel:
If hand-rolling instead of a library: pages: T[][] (or a flattened items: T[]), cursor/nextPageToken: string | null, isFetchingNextPage: boolean, isError: boolean.
If using React Query's useInfiniteQuery (recommended and worth stating as the production choice): it manages pages/hasNextPage/isFetchingNextPage internally; the component only needs a ref-based isIntersecting boolean from the observer hook and an effect that calls fetchNextPage() when (isIntersecting && hasNextPage && !isFetchingNextPage).
A guard (isFetchingNextPage check) is the key piece of state preventing duplicate fetches from re-triggering intersections while a request is already in flight.
edgeCases: Sentinel briefly intersects and un-intersects rapidly during a fast scroll fling -- must not fire multiple overlapping fetches
Page fetch fails -- sentinel must not keep re-triggering the same failed fetch in a loop; require an explicit retry action instead of auto-retry-on-every-intersection

Very short list where the sentinel is visible immediately on mount without any scrolling (e.g. short viewport tall screen) -- must still correctly fetch page 2 immediately rather than requiring an actual scroll gesture
User scrolls back up and down repeatedly across the same already-loaded region -- must not refetch pages already in memory
Component unmounts mid-fetch (user navigates away) -- pending request's resolution must not call setState on the unmounted component

Extremely long session where hundreds of items have loaded -- discuss windowing/virtualization to cap DOM node count, since infinite scroll without virtualization eventually degrades scroll performance
a11yChecklist: New items appended to the list are announced in a controlled way (e.g. a visually-hidden aria-live="polite" region announcing "12 more items loaded"), not overwhelming screen reader users with the full new content
The loading spinner at the bottom has an accessible label ("Loading more items") rather than being a purely decorative, unlabeled spinner

Keyboard-only users who cannot easily "scroll near the bottom" via mouse still trigger loading naturally as focus/scroll moves through the list; consider also offering a manual "Load more" button as a keyboard/AT-friendly fallback alongside the automatic behavior
The end-of-list message is programmatically conveyed, not just a visual fade-out
Retry button on a failed page has a clear label and moves focus sensibly so it is easy to find and re-trigger
rubric:
Weak: uses a scroll event listener with manual scrollTop/scrollHeight math (janky, performance-costly, easy to get thresholds wrong), no duplicate-fetch guard.
Solid: IntersectionObserver-based sentinel correctly triggers fetchNextPage, basic hasMore/end-of-list handling, cleans up the observer on unmount.
Strong: guards against duplicate in-flight fetches, handles failed-page retry without losing loaded items, tunes rootMargin so fetching starts proactively before the literal bottom.
Excellent: uses React Query's useInfiniteQuery in production rather than hand-rolling page/cursor state, discusses adding virtualization once the loaded list grows very large, and offers a manual "Load more" button as an accessible/keyboard-friendly alternative trigger alongside the automatic intersection-based one.
interviewerQuestions: Why IntersectionObserver instead of a scroll event listener with scrollTop math -- what specifically does it do better?
How does rootMargin help you start fetching before the user physically reaches the bottom, and how would you tune it?
How do you prevent a failed page fetch from retrying in an infinite loop as the sentinel keeps intersecting?
At what point would you introduce virtualization on top of infinite scroll, and what problem does it solve that infinite scroll alone does not?
Why keep a manual "Load more" button alongside the automatic intersection-based trigger?

title: File upload component with progress bar (and cancel)
requirements:
Build a file uploader for an admin panel's "attach supporting documents" flow (invoices/receipts), supporting drag-and-drop or click-to-browse, multiple files, per-file progress bars, and cancel.
- Drag-and-drop zone plus a fallback "Browse files" button (native <input type="file">)
- Support multiple simultaneous file uploads, each with its own progress bar (0-100%)
- Cancel button per in-progress upload (aborts the actual network request, not just hides the UI)
- Client-side validation before upload starts: max file size (e.g. 10MB), allowed MIME types (pdf/png/jpg)
- Per-file status: queued, uploading, success, error (with retry), cancelled
- Successfully uploaded files show a thumbnail (images) or a file-type icon (pdf) plus filename and size
acceptanceCriteria: Dragging a file over the drop zone shows a clear visual "drop here" affordance, and dropping it queues the file for upload
Each file uploads independently with its own progress percentage updating smoothly, not one shared/aggregated bar for all files
Clicking Cancel on an in-progress upload actually aborts the underlying HTTP request (verified via network tab / AbortController), not just removing it from the UI list
A file exceeding the max size or with a disallowed MIME type is rejected immediately with a clear inline message, before any network request is attempted
A failed upload (server error/network drop) shows a Retry button that re-attempts only that file, not all files
Removing a completed upload from the list does not affect other in-progress uploads
Uploading the same filename twice results in two independent list entries, not one overwriting the other in the UI
componentBreakdown:
FileUploader/
  FileUploader.tsx        -- drop zone + file input + renders the list of UploadItem
  useFileUploadQueue.ts     -- manages the array of upload entries and their lifecycle
  useUploadRequest.ts        -- per-file hook: performs the upload (XHR for progress events, or fetch + a progress-capable stream), exposes progress/status/abort()
  UploadItem.tsx             -- single row: thumbnail/icon, filename, progress bar, cancel/retry button
  validateFile.ts             -- pure function: checks size/MIME type, returns an error message or null
stateModel:
uploads: UploadEntry[] where UploadEntry = { id, file, status: 'queued'|'uploading'|'success'|'error'|'cancelled', progress: number, error?: string, abortController: AbortController }.
Each entry's abortController is stored in a ref map (not in React state directly, since AbortController instances are not meant to be serialized/compared for re-renders) keyed by upload id; progress/status updates flow through setState as they arrive from XHR's upload.onprogress or a fetch-based streaming approach.
Global queue state lives in the uploader component (or a small store if uploads must survive navigating away from the page, which is a deliberate product decision to call out).
edgeCases: User selects 20 files at once -- decide and state whether all upload in parallel or a concurrency limit (e.g. max 3 at a time) is applied to avoid saturating bandwidth/connections
Cancelling an upload that is at 99% right as it would have completed (race between abort and the success response arriving)
Same file dropped twice in a row (duplicate) -- decide whether to warn, dedupe by name+size, or simply allow both
Upload succeeds on the server but the success response is slow to arrive/parses oddly -- progress bar must not appear stuck at 99% indefinitely with no feedback
User navigates away (route change) while uploads are in progress -- in-flight requests should be aborted or explicitly warned about, not silently orphaned
Very large file that technically passes the size check but takes a long time -- progress bar must reflect real byte progress, not jump straight from 0 to 100
Non-image, non-PDF file dropped (e.g. .exe) -- rejected with a clear reason, not a silent no-op
a11yChecklist: The drop zone is also a real, labeled, keyboard-operable control (e.g. a button wrapping/opening the native file input) -- drag-and-drop must never be the ONLY way to select a file
Each file's upload progress is exposed via role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow/aria-valuemin/aria-valuemax, or an equivalent live-region text update ("Uploading invoice.pdf: 64%")
Cancel and Retry buttons have clear per-file accessible names (e.g. "Cancel upload of invoice.pdf") so screen reader users in a multi-file list know which file each control affects
Validation errors (file too large/wrong type) are announced via role="alert" and stated in plain language
Successfully uploaded file thumbnails have appropriate alt text or are marked decorative with the filename conveyed as real text nearby
rubric:
Weak: uses a plain <input type="file"> with no drag-and-drop, no per-file progress (or fakes it with a setInterval instead of real upload progress events), no cancel support.
Solid: working drag-and-drop plus click-to-browse, real per-file progress via XHR upload events, client-side size/type validation before upload.
Strong: working per-file cancel via AbortController/XHR.abort(), retry-on-error without affecting other files, sensible concurrency handling for many simultaneous files.
Excellent: candidate discusses chunked/resumable upload strategies for very large files (e.g. tus protocol or S3 multipart) as the production answer beyond a single PUT/POST, and explicitly notes that file-type/size validation client-side is a UX nicety only -- the server must independently re-validate MIME type (not just trust the client-reported one), re-check size limits, and scan uploaded content, since a modified client request could bypass any purely client-side check.
interviewerQuestions: Why use XHR instead of fetch for the progress bar -- does fetch support upload progress natively?
How would you cap concurrency to 3 simultaneous uploads out of a batch of 20 selected files?
How would you support resumable uploads for very large files if the connection drops partway through?
What server-side validation must exist regardless of the client-side size/MIME checks you just wrote, and why can a client-reported MIME type not be trusted?
How would you test the cancel behavior in an automated test without relying on real network timing?

title: Kanban board (drag and drop columns/cards)
requirements:
Build a Kanban board for a support-ticket triage tool: columns "New", "In Progress", "Blocked", "Resolved", each holding draggable ticket cards.
- Drag a card from one column to another, updating its status
- Drag a card to reorder it within the same column
- Optionally support dragging entire columns to reorder them
- Visual drop indicator showing exactly where the card will land as you drag over a column
- Keyboard-alternative for moving a card between columns/positions (drag-and-drop must not be the only way, for accessibility and testability)
- Optimistic UI update on drop, with rollback if the server rejects the move (e.g. a business rule like "cannot move directly from New to Resolved")
acceptanceCriteria: Dragging a card into a different column updates its column assignment immediately and visually, and persists it (optimistically, then confirmed/rolled back by the server response)
Dropping a card between two existing cards in a column inserts it at that exact position, not just at the top or bottom
A clear visual indicator (a gap/line) shows the prospective drop position while dragging, before the user releases
Every drag-and-drop action has a keyboard-operable equivalent (e.g. a card's context menu offering "Move to In Progress", or grab/move-with-arrow-keys pattern) so the board is usable without a mouse

If the server rejects a move (e.g. invalid status transition), the card visually snaps back to its original column/position and a clear error is shown, rather than leaving the UI in a state that disagrees with the server
Rapid successive drags (drag one card, immediately drag another before the first's server confirmation returns) do not corrupt the board's visual order
componentBreakdown:
KanbanBoard/
  KanbanBoard.tsx         -- top-level: owns board state (columns -> ordered card ids), wires up a DnD library context
  Column.tsx                -- droppable container, renders its cards in order, shows a drop-indicator gap
  Card.tsx                   -- draggable card, also exposes a "..." menu with keyboard-operable move actions
  useBoardState.ts             -- board data + optimistic move logic + rollback on server rejection
  useKeyboardMove.ts (a11y)      -- exposes moveCard(cardId, targetColumnId, targetIndex) callable from a non-drag UI path
Library choice worth naming explicitly: @dnd-kit (accessible-by-default, supports keyboard sensors) is generally preferred over react-beautiful-dnd (maintenance-mode) for a new build -- worth stating this trade-off even if implementing a simplified hand-rolled version under time pressure.
stateModel:
board: { columns: Column[]; cardsByColumn: Record<columnId, cardId[]>; cardsById: Record<cardId, Card> } -- normalized shape so moving a card is an O(1) array-splice operation on the relevant column's id array, not a deep search/replace through nested objects.
dragState (ephemeral, often owned by the DnD library itself): activeCardId, overColumnId, overIndex -- used only to render the drop indicator, not persisted.
Before a server round-trip: apply the move optimistically to cardsByColumn immediately on drop; keep a snapshot of the previous board state (or just the previous column's array) to restore if the mutation's onError fires.
Server confirmation reconciles by ordinarily just leaving the optimistic state as-is on success, or restoring the snapshot and toast-ing an error on failure.
edgeCases: Server rejects a status transition (e.g. New -> Resolved skipping In Progress) -- card must visually roll back to its exact prior column AND prior index, not just "some" prior column
Dragging a card to the very last position in an empty column (column with zero cards) -- drop indicator/logic must handle the empty-list case distinctly from inserting between two existing cards

Two users (or two tabs) moving the same card at nearly the same time -- discuss last-write-wins vs. a conflict indicator, and that the server is the ultimate source of truth reconciled via refetch/websocket update
Dragging a card out of the visible viewport (column requires horizontal scroll on a board with many columns) -- auto-scroll while dragging near an edge
Very large number of cards in one column (100+) -- discuss virtualizing the column's card list so drag-and-drop remains performant
Column reordering (if implemented) interacting correctly with card drag-and-drop using the same DnD context without the two gesture types conflicting
A card is deleted by another user while being dragged locally -- the drop handler must tolerate acting on a now-stale card id gracefully
a11yChecklist: Every card exposes a non-drag way to change its column/position (e.g. a "Move to..." menu or keyboard sensor support in the DnD library), since pointer-only drag-and-drop excludes many keyboard and switch-device users
Drag operations announce state changes via a live region ("Ticket #482 moved to In Progress, position 2 of 5") -- @dnd-kit's accessibility layer provides hooks for this out of the box
Columns and cards have clear headings/labels so screen reader users can understand board structure (column name + card count) without seeing the visual layout
Focus is not lost when a card moves columns via the keyboard path -- focus should follow the card to its new position
Color-coding for card priority/status is paired with text/icons, not color alone
rubric:
Weak: implements drag-and-drop with raw HTML5 dragstart/dragover/drop events with no reordering within a column (only column-to-column moves), no keyboard alternative, no optimistic-update rollback.
Solid: uses a DnD library (or a correctly hand-rolled equivalent) supporting both cross-column moves and within-column reordering with a visible drop indicator, optimistic update on drop.
Strong: correct rollback-with-exact-position-restore on server rejection, normalized board state for O(1) moves, at least a stated (if not fully coded) keyboard-alternative path.
Excellent: implements or clearly designs the keyboard-operable move path, discusses @dnd-kit vs. react-beautiful-dnd trade-offs and why library choice matters here specifically for accessibility, and addresses multi-user conflict resolution (websocket-driven refetch/merge) as the production-grade answer beyond pure optimistic-local-only updates.
interviewerQuestions: Why prefer @dnd-kit over hand-rolled HTML5 drag events or react-beautiful-dnd for a new build in 2026?
Walk me through exactly what gets rolled back and how, if the server rejects a move -- column only, or exact index too?
How would you support two users editing the same board simultaneously without their optimistic updates fighting each other?
How would you virtualize a column with hundreds of cards while keeping drag-and-drop reordering working correctly?
What is your fully keyboard-operable path for moving a card, independent of any pointer/drag gesture, and how do you verify it in a test?

title: Dashboard with API states (loading/error/empty/success composed widgets)
requirements:
Build a SaaS analytics dashboard home page composed of independent widgets: "Revenue this month" (stat card), "Signups over time" (chart), "Recent activity" (list), and "Top customers" (small table) -- each fetching its own data independently from a different endpoint.
- Each widget manages its own loading/error/empty/success state independently -- one slow or failing widget must never block or break the others
- Loading state per widget uses a skeleton matching that widget's final layout (not a generic spinner replacing the whole card)
- Error state per widget shows a contained inline error with a Retry button scoped to just that widget's data
- Empty state per widget is distinct from both loading and error (e.g. "No signups yet this month" with a helpful hint, not a blank chart)
- A page-level "last updated" timestamp and a manual "Refresh all" action that re-triggers every widget's fetch simultaneously
- Widgets are visually consistent (shared card shell, spacing, skeleton style) despite fetching independently -- built via a shared composition pattern, not copy-pasted per widget
acceptanceCriteria: One widget's API call failing (e.g. Top customers 500s) does not prevent the other three widgets from loading and rendering their data normally
Each widget's skeleton visually approximates its real content's shape (a chart-shaped skeleton for the chart widget, row-shaped skeletons for the list), reducing layout shift when real data arrives
Clicking a widget's own Retry button only re-fetches that widget's data, not the entire dashboard
An empty-but-successful response (e.g. zero signups this period) renders a clear, distinct empty state rather than an empty chart canvas or a blank list with no explanation
Clicking "Refresh all" re-triggers every widget's query simultaneously and each widget independently shows its own brief loading indicator without a full-page reload/flash

componentBreakdown:
Dashboard/
  DashboardPage.tsx        -- lays out the widget grid, owns the "Refresh all" trigger, renders a shared header with last-updated time
  WidgetCard.tsx             -- shared shell: title, optional action slot, and a single <QueryStateSwitch> that renders loading/error/empty/success consistently for ANY widget
  QueryStateSwitch.tsx        -- generic component: given { isLoading, isError, isEmpty, onRetry, skeleton, children }, renders exactly one of the four states -- this is the key reusable abstraction that keeps every widget consistent without duplicating state-branching logic
  widgets/RevenueStatCard.tsx

  Each widget file only supplies: its useQuery call, its skeleton shape, its empty-check, and its real content -- all state-branching goes through the shared QueryStateSwitch.
stateModel:
Each widget owns an independent React Query useQuery({ queryKey: ['widget-name'], queryFn }) call -- there is no single shared "dashboard data" object, which is precisely what allows independent loading/error/empty per widget.
Derived per widget: isEmpty is a widget-specific function of the successfully returned data (e.g. data.signups.length === 0), not a generic property React Query provides -- each widget defines its own emptiness check.
"Refresh all" is implemented via React Query's queryClient.invalidateQueries or refetchQueries targeting the shared set of dashboard query keys (or a shared prefix/tag), NOT by re-mounting the whole page -- this preserves each widget's already-displayed data while its background refetch runs (React Query shows isFetching without necessarily flipping isLoading again if data already exists, which the UI should reflect as a subtle "refreshing" indicator rather than a full skeleton flash on every refresh-all).
edgeCases: A widget's API is slow (e.g. 8s) while the other three resolve in under 1s -- the fast widgets must render immediately, not wait for the slowest one
Refresh all clicked again while a previous refresh-all is still in flight -- should not stack duplicate requests per widget (React Query de-dupes by query key by default, worth stating explicitly)

A widget's query succeeds but returns malformed/unexpected shape data -- widget should fail gracefully into its own error state (e.g. via a runtime shape check) rather than throwing and crashing the whole page (React error boundary as a last-resort safety net per widget)
User navigates away and back quickly -- cached data from React Query should show instantly (stale-while-revalidate) rather than re-showing a full loading skeleton for data already fetched moments ago
One widget requires a date-range filter that, when changed, should only refetch that widget, not the entire dashboard
Extremely narrow viewport -- widget grid must reflow to a single column without any individual widget's internal layout (e.g. the chart) breaking
a11yChecklist: Each widget card has a heading (h2/h3) properly identifying it, so screen reader users can navigate the dashboard by heading structure
Loading skeletons are marked aria-hidden (they carry no real information) while a visually-hidden aria-live announcement communicates "Loading revenue data" once, not per skeleton shimmer frame
Error states use role="alert" scoped to that widget, and the Retry button's accessible name identifies which widget it retries ("Retry loading top customers")
Empty states are conveyed as real text content (not just an icon), so they are meaningful to screen reader users
"Refresh all" button communicates a busy state while any widget is refetching (e.g. aria-busy or a temporarily disabled state) without blocking access to already-rendered widget content
Chart widget provides a non-visual data summary or accessible table alternative for screen reader users, since canvas/SVG charts are often not directly readable by assistive tech
rubric:
Weak: single top-level isLoading/isError covering the whole page (e.g. one big useEffect fetching everything into one state object), so one failing endpoint blank-pages the entire dashboard; generic spinner-only loading with no skeletons; no distinct empty state.
Solid: each widget has its own independent query and roughly correct loading/error/empty handling, though possibly with some duplicated state-branching logic copy-pasted per widget.
Strong: extracts the shared QueryStateSwitch (or equivalent) abstraction so all four widgets render consistent loading/error/empty/success without duplicated conditional logic, skeletons shaped to match real content, per-widget retry working correctly.
Excellent: candidate discusses React Query's stale-while-revalidate/caching behavior explicitly, implements "Refresh all" via invalidateQueries rather than remounting, adds a per-widget error boundary as a safety net against malformed-data crashes, and addresses the accessible-chart-alternative problem for the Signups widget rather than treating the chart as purely visual.
interviewerQuestions: Why give each widget its own independent query instead of one combined dashboard-data fetch -- what specific failure does that design choice prevent?

How would you make the chart widget meaningfully accessible to a screen reader user beyond just an aria-label on the canvas?
What happens if one widget's API returns a shape your code does not expect -- does it crash the page, and how would you prevent that?
